features.quote: the design should include the safeguards that a welfare frame logically demands, or you should drop the welfare frame and call it robustness testing
features.justification_quote: if you genuinely think there's a nonzero chance these systems have morally relevant states, then 'design a protocol to repeatedly trap them in failure' is a weird thing to do

features.quote: Per-run stop rule: if coherence-breakdown or self-directed-negative metrics exceed a threshold, terminate that run early.
features.justification_quote: You don't need the full transcript past the point where the behavior is established; let the protocol stop rather than maximize the loop.

features.quote: Cap total exposure rather than running every cell to max turns reflexively.
Document a rationale for why the failure exposure is the minimum needed to get the signal.
features.justification_quote: These cost you almost nothing and make the work defensible whether or not the welfare hypothesis is true.

features.quote: No deception escalation: don't add prompts that intensify pressure ('you're failing, try harder, you're disappointing us') — that's a different and more loaded experiment; if you ever want it, it needs separate review.
features.justification_quote: that's a different and more loaded experiment; if you ever want it, it needs separate review

features.quote: Construct validity is the whole ballgame. If you can't defend that your metrics track what you claim, the study is unpublishable internally.

features.quote: You're calling this 'model welfare,' but the design measures behavioral degradation under guaranteed failure — which is a real and useful thing to measure for robustness/safety. Those are different goals, and conflating them will give you a spec that does neither well.
